title: 38-21_Gr. of Draper
text:
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
GRIEVANCE OF )
SHAWN DRAPER ) DOCKET NO. 23-16
FINDINGS OF FACT, OPINION, AND ORDER
Vermont State Employees’ Association (“VSEA” “Union”) filed a Grievance on behalf
of Shawn Draper (“Mr. Draper” “Grievant”) alleging the Vermont Department of Transportation
violated Article 47 of the Collective Bargaining Agreement between the parties when it denied
Grievant higher assignment pay (“HAP”) on days when he substituted for his supervisor.
The Vermont Labor Relations Board (“Board”) held a hearing on August 22, 2024,
before Board members, Robert Greemore, Chair, Karen Saudek1, and Roger Donegan. The
Grievant appeared and was represented by G. Alexander Robertson, Esq. The Department of
Transportation was represented by Assistant Attorney General William Reynolds. The parties
filed post hearing briefs on December 30, 2024.
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. Grievant Shawn Draper is employed by the Agency of Transportation as a Senior
Operations Technician (“TSOT”) at the Dummerston garage.
2. Mr. Draper began working for AOT in 2001 as an Equipment Specialist. He has held the
TSOT position, previously called the Transportation Senior Maintenance Worker
position, since about 2014.
1 Board member Karen Saudek participated at the hearing, but did not participate in the
deliberations in this matter. See Section 11.15 Vermont Labor Relations Board Rules of Practice
(“The presence of two Board members constitutes a quorum with authority to conduct hearings
and to act.”).
21

3. The TSOT job classification is part of a series of job classifications referred to as the
Transportation Operations Technician (“TOT”) series, formerly the Transportation
Maintenance Worker series. These employees maintain the state roads including
clearing snow and litter and installing culverts and guardrails. The TSOTs are at the top
of the TOT hierarchy, below them are three TOT classifications I-III.
4. Grievant’s supervisor is Transportation Area Maintenance Supervisor (“TAMS”) II
Christopher Berg.
5. The TAMS is responsible for supervising the TOTS and TSOTs. The TAMS spends
time at the garage completing administrative duties. The TAMs also oversee work in the
field.
6. For off-hour operation issues, AOT contacts the TAMS first and if they are not available,
TAMS Berg forwards these calls to the TSOTs. Examples of incidents warranting these
off-hour calls are accidents, road closures, or animals hit on the roadway.
7. TSOT Draper has substituted for TAMS Berg in the latter’s absence. Grievant estimates
he has served in this capacity four or five times per year.
8. Before the fall of 2022, Grievant received higher assignment pay (“HAP”) when he
filled in or substituted for TAMS Berg. The difference in pay grade between Mr. Draper
and his supervisor was three pay grades.
9. On 8/5/21, AOT Operations Director Gammell and Deputy Director Law filed a Request
for Classification Review (“RFR”) for each of the four maintenance worker
classifications, including Grievant’s position, to accurately reflect the work and
responsibilities of these employees.
10. The RFR included a suggested four pay grade increase for Senor Maintenance Worker
22

classification from pay grade 20 to pay grade 24. The RFR outlined the following
responsibilities for the TSOT position “must provide all the duties of a TAMS in this
capacity without the supervisory title. In the absence of the TAMS (vacation, etc.) they
do perform the supervisory role.” Exhibit D.
11. Part of the impetus for the RFRs was to make AOT operation positions more
competitive and improve recruitment.
12. In drafting the RFRs Director Gammell and Deputy Director Law asked the District
Transportation Administrators, who were more familiar with the work performed by
their staff, to provide the first draft of the RFRs.
13. Many of the positions described duties and responsibilities that the workers had already
been performing for several years before the RFRs were filed. For years, the Senior
Maintenance Workers had been substituting for the area supervisor when the supervisor
was out. The Senior Maintenance Workers were the second in command.
14. The four positions for which RFRs were filed were the equivalent of the apprentice,
journeyman, master, and senior maintenance worker.
15. As part of the RFR process, AOT management distributed the RFR forms and draft job
specifications to the affected employees during a series of meetings called “tailgate
talks.”
16. On August 19, 2021, Grievant attended a “Tailgate Talk” at Dummerston Garage with
Shannon Gilberts, the acting General Manager for District 2. Gilbert brought the four
RFRs and job specifications to the meeting and left them for the employees to review.
23

17. Grievant was informed that his position and the other positions would be upgraded by
four pay grades. Grievant understood that the process was not completed and approvals
needed to be obtained.
18. Grievant recalled that “they put down the papers” for each of the positions, but did not
remember seeing the RFR documents.
19. Grievant signed a document acknowledging that he attended the Tailgate Talk, that the
different maintenance series RFRs were available for his review, and the duties of each
had been reviewed with him. “By signing below you are acknowledging that at this
Tailgate Talk on, 8-19-21, a supervisor or manager went over the class review RFRs for
the maintenance worker series.” Exhibit E.
20. The AOT Classification Committee (“Committee”) reviews RFRs. The Committee is
comprised of ten employees from AOT and the Department of Human Resources. On or
about September 21, 2021, the Committee met to review the RFR for the Transportation
Senior Maintenance Worker classification.
21. Initially, the Committee did not reach consensus on approving a pay grade increase to 24
because of questions about the level of knowledge, skill, and mental demand required
for the senior maintenance employees and requested additional information from
Director Gammell and Deputy Director Law.
22. Director Gammell and Deputy Director Law met with the Committee to answer
questions about the level of supervision and whether the Senior Maintenance Workers
would be expected to take on the higher-level duties of a supervisor in the absence of
their supervisor. Director Gammell and Deputy Director Law reported that the Senior
Maintenance Workers did fill in as acting supervisors and performed these higher level
24

duties.
23. The Committee requested that the class specification for the position be changed to
include: “[a]lso serves as a regular replacement for an AOT Maintenance Supervisor I
and/or II in their absence.” Satisfied with the change, the Committee agreed to upgrade
the pay grade for the position to 24.
24. On November 5, 2021, the Committee released a Notice of Classification Action to AOT
indicating the change in job title for the AOT Senior Maintenance Worker to
Transportation Senior Ops Tech and a change in pay grade from 20 to pay grade 24. The
effective date of the change was August 15, 2021.
25. It is not common for pay grades to increase by four points.
26. The pay upgrades were based in part on the need to recruit more people for maintenance
positions.
27. The Area Supervisor pay grade also went up three pay grades to a pay grade 27.
28. There was no input from AOT Human Resources or central office to change the
classification to include the requirement of serving as a regular replacement for an AOT
Maintenance Supervisor I and/or II in their absence.
29. In August 2021, negotiations began between VSEA and the State for the non-
management bargaining unit for the successor contract effective July 1, 2022-June 30,
2024. Gary Hoadley was the lead negotiator for VSEA, John Berard and Joe McNeil
were the lead negotiators for the State.
30. Deputy Director Law was not involved in the negotiations for the non-bargaining unit
taking place in the late summer and fall of 2021. He does not believe Director Gammel
was involved in the negotiation process.
25

31. The 2021 negotiations completed in October 2021, leading to an Agreement exchanged
on October 27, and executed on October 28, 2021.
32. The Union and State negotiated a collective bargaining agreement for non-management
unit effective July 1, 2022-June 30, 2024. Article 47 of the Non-Management
Bargaining Unit Contract addresses HAP and includes the following:
1. An employee who, in the absence of an incumbent, is assigned by the
appointing authority:
(a) To perform a majority of those duties of the higher level job which are
substantially different from his or her own duties; or,
(b) To assume the responsibilities of a higher level supervisory or managerial
job without any substantial change in duties; shall, commencing with the
third consecutive workday in which the employee actually worked a full shift,
be eligible for higher assignment pay, retroactive to the first day worked.
. . . .
7. Employees in the following categories shall not be eligible:
(a) positions designated as trainee classes
(b) automatic promotion classes
(c) employees whose class specifications clearly require them to fill in and
assume the higher level duties.
8. Employees assuming a supervisory position in an institution where the policy
requires such a person to be in a “charge” or command position, shall be eligible
for this differential for each full shift actually worked, and shall not be subject to
the three (3) consecutive days eligibility criteria in Section 1, above.
Gr. Ex. 1, at 63-64 (emphasis added).
33. Changes to Article 47 resulted in a reduction in the number of days needed to qualify for
Higher Assignment pay, from five to three. This Union gain was reached in exchange
for the Union agreeing to changes in the Commercial Driver’s License and emergency
closing articles.
34. The description of the ineligible positions in Section 7 of Article 47 did not change as a
result of the negotiations in 2021.
35. Grievant was assigned to perform duties of his supervisor TAMS Berg during his
26

absence from October 3, 2022, through October 15, 2022.
36. Grievant did not receive higher assignment pay while performing the duties of his
supervisor Berg from October 3, 2022, through October 15, 2022.
37. Grievant was assigned by AOT to perform the duties of his supervisor TAMS Berg
during his absence from November 21, 2022, through November 25, 2022.
38. Grievant did not receive higher assignment pay while performing the duties of Berg
from November 21, 2022, through November 25, 2022.
OPINION
Grievant claims the State violated Article 47 of the Collective Bargaining Agreement
(“CBA”) when it relied on the TSOT class specification to deny HAP to him. Grievant claims
the exception to HAP outlined in Section 7(c) of Article 47 does not apply to the circumstances
where an employee is substituting for their supervisor and otherwise eligible for HAP under
Section 1(b) of Article 47. Even if 7(c) applies to employees substituting for their employees,
the Union assets, it does not apply here because the reclassification did not result in a material
change because Senior Maintenance Workers, now TSOTs, substituted for their supervisors
before the reclassification. Finally, Grievant asserts the State should be estopped from applying
the HAP exclusion to Grievant and other TSOTs.
The State contends the Union has failed to sustain its burden of proving the State violated
the CBA, which is clear and unambiguous and excludes Grievant from HAP because his class
specification clearly requires him to fill in and assume the higher-level duties of his supervisor.
The Grievant has the burden of proving the Employer breached the CBA. When
interpreting the provisions of collective bargaining agreements in resolving grievances, the
Board follows the rules of contract construction developed by the Vermont Supreme Court. The
27

cardinal principle in the construction of any contract is to give effect to the true intention of the
parties. Grievance of Cronan, et al, 151 Vt. 576, 579 (1989). A contract must be construed, if
possible, to give effect to every part, and from the parts to form a harmonious whole. In re
Grievance of VSEA on Behalf of “Phase Down” Employees, 139 Vt. 63, 65 (1980). The contract
provisions must be viewed in their entirety and read together. In re Stacey, 138 Vt. 68, 72 (1980).
A contract will be interpreted by the common meaning of its words where the language is
clear. Id. at 71. If clear and unambiguous, the provisions of a contract must be given force and
effect and be taken in their plain, ordinary, and popular sense. Swett v. Vermont State Colleges,
141 Vt. 275, 277 (1982). If analysis of the contract language results in a determination that the
language is clear and unambiguous, extrinsic evidence should not be considered as it would alter
the understanding of the parties embodied in the language they chose to best express their intent.
Hackel v. Vermont State Colleges, 140 Vt. 446, 452 (1981). The Board will not read terms into a
contract unless they arise by necessary implication. In re Stacey, 138 Vt. at 71. The law will
presume that the parties meant, and intended to be bound by, the plain and express language of
their undertakings. Vermont State Colleges Fac. Fed'n, VFT, AFT, Loc. No. 3180, AFL-CIO v.
Vermont State Colleges, 141 Vt. 138, 144 (1982). The Board has a duty to construe contracts;
not to make or remake them for the parties or ignore their provisions. See Id.
Ambiguity exists where the disputed language will allow more than one reasonable
interpretation. In re Grievance of VSEA & Dargie, 179 Vt. 228, 234 (2005). The threshold
question of whether a contract is ambiguous is a question of law. Isbrandtsen v. North Branch
Corp., 150 Vt. 575, 577 (1988). In making this determination, we may consider evidence as to
the circumstances surrounding the making of the agreement as well as the object, nature and
subject matter of the writing. In re Spear, 2014 VT 57, ¶ 15, 196 Vt. 517.
28

The contract provision in dispute, Article 47, Section 7 (c), provides in pertinent part,
that “[e]mployees in the following categories shall not be eligible: . . . (c) employees whose class
specifications clearly require them to fill in and assume the higher level duties.” Article 47,
⁋7(c).The Union argues the language in Section 7(c),“is at least ambiguous as to whether it
extends to employees substituting for a supervisory position.” Union’s Brief at 14. The Union
asserts the term “duties” is ambiguous because Article 47 creates a distinction between “duties”
and assumption of supervisory “responsibilities.” The qualifying provision for HAP under 1 (b),
includes the term “responsibilities.” Section 1 (b) identifies employees eligible for higher
assignment pay, “who in the absence of an incumbent is assigned by the appointing authority: (b)
to assume the responsibilities of a higher level supervisory or managerial job without any
substantial change in duties . . . .” Because the limiting or disqualifying language in Section 7(c)
does not mention responsibilities, the Union argues, 7 (c) does not or cannot apply to the
employees qualifying for HAP under 1(b).
The plain and ordinary meaning of “duties” refers to “any action, task, etc., required by
or relating to one’s occupation or position.” Webster’s New World Dictionary of American
English (3d. Ed. 1988), at 42. The term “duties” in 7(c) of Article 47, does not exclude
supervisory responsibilities. On the contrary, the “duties” contained in 7(c) refers to those of the
“higher level supervisory or managerial job” to which they are assigned in the absence of the
incumbent. There is nothing ambiguous or confusing about this provision or the term “duties.”
The fact that the word “responsibilities” is included in the eligibility section, but not in the
exclusionary section does not render the latter section ambiguous. The exclusionary section
seeks to limit or exclude some of those employees otherwise qualifying under the broader section
of 1 (b). It is reasonable and not confusing that the language in 7(c) does not mirror, and is less
29

broad, than that found in 1(b). The term “duties” is not ambiguous or confusing and the Board
will apply Article 47, and the plain and ordinary meaning of its exclusionary Section 7(c).
Application of Section 7(c) to Grievant’s class specification demonstrates that he is not
entitled to HAP for the time he filled in for his supervisor in October and November 2022. The
class specification for Grievant’s position of Transportation Senor Operations Technician was
changed in 2021, to include the following: “also serves as a regular replacement for an AOT
Area Maintenance Supervisor I and/or II in their absence.” The class specification clearly
provides that Grievant should replace, fill-in, and perform the duties of his supervisor. Grievant
was not eligible for HAP when he filled in for his supervisor in October and November 2022.
The Union also relies on amendments made thirty years ago as supporting its claim the
parties intended that employees substituting for their supervisors should be eligible for HAP.
Neither the Union nor the State offered testimony that detailed or described the intent of the
parties at the time of drafting these earlier iterations. Moreover, the intent of the parties is best
determined by reviewing the words chosen in the applicable Collective Bargaining Agreement.
The Board has concluded the language of the applicable contract is clear and unambiguous and
the parties agreed to exclude from HAP those employees whose class specification clearly
required them to fill in and assume “the higher level duties.” Higher level duties include filling
in for a supervisor.
The Union also claims past practice does not support excluding HAP where employees
assume supervisor roles, because the State cites only one past practice. Where the language of
the contract is clear and unambiguous, the Board will apply its plain and ordinary terms and will
not resort to extrinsic evidence of bargaining history and past practice. See generally Grievance
30

of Vermont State Employees' Association (re: Annual Leave Accruals), 33 VLRB 330, 340
(2016).
The Union also asserts that the HAP exception should not apply here because the
classification change was a mere paper change to a job description without any connection to
classification review. The Union claims that “changes to a class specification should be
operative in denying HAP eligibility only if they materially informed a reclassification position.”
Union’s brief at 23. Although there is nothing in Article 47 that supports such a limitation, even
if the Board were to consider such an interpretation, the facts in the classification review for the
TSOT support application of the exclusion. The facts demonstrate that although the senior
maintenance workers had been substituting for their supervisors for years, to support the four
steps pay grade increase, the Classification Committee required the inclusion of language in the
specification that they “[a]lso serves as a regular replacement for an AOT Maintenance
Supervisor I and/or II in their absence.” Exhibit C. The inclusion of this language materially
informed the reclassification of Grievant’s position.
Finally, the Union claims that equitable estoppel should prevent the State from applying
the exclusion provision to Grievant and award him HAP pay. The use of equitable estoppel
against the government is rare and should only be used in extraordinary circumstances. See In re
Langlois/Novicki Variance Denial, 2017 VT 76, ¶ 27, 205 Vt. 340, 352. The party seeking
equitable estoppel against the government must establish all four of the elements of estoppel: (1)
the party to be estopped must know the facts; (2) the party being estopped must intend that their
conduct shall be acted upon; (3) the party asserting estoppel must be ignorant of the true facts;
and (4) the party asserting the estoppel must rely on the conduct of the party to be estopped to his
detriment. See Wesco, Inc. v. City of Montpelier, 169 Vt. 520, 524 (1999). Additionally, the
31

party seeking to estop the government must demonstrate that “the injustice that would ensue
from a failure to find an estoppel sufficiently outweighs any effect upon public interest or policy
that would result from estopping the government in a particular case.” In re Letourneau, 168 Vt.
539, 547 (1998) (quotations omitted).
The Union has failed to demonstrate the requisite elements of estoppel. There is no
evidence that the State bargaining representatives knew about the change to the TSOT class
specification that was recommended and approved by the Classification Committee. The State
did not have superior knowledge or withheld that knowledge from the Union. The State
representative John Berard testified that he learned of the reclassification of the maintenance
worker positions after bargaining had been concluded. This information did not inform the
contract negotiations between the State and VSEA. The State did not mislead or misrepresent
the status of that process or the results of that process. The Union cannot demonstrate that it was
ignorant of the true facts. The Union was aware that a potential reclassification was pending
during its negotiations.
Because the Union has not satisfied the elements of estoppel, the Board is not required
to balance the equities.
32

ORDER
Based on the foregoing findings of fact and for foregoing reasons, it is ordered that the
Grievance of Shawn Draper is DISMISSED.
Dated this 1st day of May 2025, at Montpelier, Vermont.
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
